attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter, stated in his own voice and not quoted from anyone else.

semantics.note: A firm present-tense observation with two parts: illegal China sales are a not-insignificant share of growth, and coverage of that growth leaves them out. The normalised wording slightly softens 'totally unmentioned in any coverage'.

contract.note: 'Parabolic growth' ordinarily means NVIDIA's multi-year growth. The contract narrows it to year-over-year growth in one quarter (Q2 FY2027), a baseline the speaker never gave. That is not the ordinary reading, and the period choice decides what evidence can count.

evidence.note: NVIDIA's own 10-Q for the target quarter. It names data center products as the growth driver but says nothing about what share came from illegal sales.
Reports a short seller's (Culper) estimate that over 20% of FY2026 compute revenue was China-driven. It covers a different period and base, and it is an allegation whose method could not be read.

A Nov 2025 FT Alphaville piece on NVIDIA's earnings that discusses probes into diversion via Singapore. This undercuts the literal 'any coverage' wording, but the contract treats earlier coverage as context only.

reviews.rationale: Nothing in the packet ties illegal transactions to a measured share of NVIDIA's recognised revenue growth, for the chosen quarter or any other. The omission claim is not settled by an archive either; e3 shows at least one earnings-related piece that raised diversion. The packet cannot settle either component.

attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence. Nearby he quotes Culper, but this sentence is his own assertion.

semantics.note: Keeps the 'more than $4.8 billion' figure and the tentative 'appears to be a passthrough' wording. 'Earnings' is used loosely: the context talks about orders of about $4.8B and about inflated revenues.

contract.note: The contract reads 'earnings' strictly as profit. The speaker's context (orders of about $4.8B, a section heading about inflated revenues) points to a revenue reading. Reading it as profit is stretched against him and changes what counts, so the interpretation does decide the result, even though the contract marks it as not decisive.

evidence.note: Megaspeed's Malaysian sister company reportedly bought at least $4.8B of AI equipment containing NVIDIA chips (Jun 2024–Feb 2026). That is a third party's equipment purchases, not NVIDIA's recognised revenue or profit, and it does not trace where the equipment ended up.

reviews.rationale: The only item gives a $4.8B figure for a third party's purchases of equipment containing NVIDIA chips. It does not measure NVIDIA's revenue or earnings from those sales, and it does not show the buyer was a passthrough to Mainland China. The figure is neither confirmed nor refuted under either reading.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter.

semantics.note: 'Advanced' and 'despite export controls' are drawn from the surrounding passage, which is about export controls and AI chips. The proposition does not require any acquisition to have been illegal.

contract.note: An ordinary reading: Chinese entities had access to NVIDIA AI GPUs across several years of the export-control era. The contract explicitly does not require proof of illegality.

evidence.note: Tom's Hardware summary of a Reuters investigation of procurement records. It reports Chinese universities buying A100s in Dec 2022 and May 2023 and about 80 A100s at Tsinghua since the ban.
DeepSeek's Dec 2024 technical report says it trained on 2,048 NVIDIA H800 GPUs, which shows actual use of a large NVIDIA cluster in China in 2024.

reviews.rationale: Documented A100 acquisitions in 2022–2023 and DeepSeek's reported H800 training cluster in 2024 show Chinese entities had and used NVIDIA AI GPUs across multiple years of the export-control era. Nothing in the packet contradicts this.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter.

semantics.note: 'Impossible to argue' is rhetorical emphasis. The underlying firm claim is that NVIDIA is selling GPUs to China through proxies and shell companies, an ongoing practice stated in the present tense.

contract.note: The speaker gave no period, and testing the present-tense claim against the latest complete month (October 2026) is a defensible convention. Treating 'selling' as downstream diversion rather than knowing participation by management is also an interpretation, and both choices shape the result.

evidence.note: Epoch AI's April 2026 estimate of large-scale smuggling to China through 2025. It is strong evidence of past diversion but says nothing about October 2026 routes.
NVIDIA's Oct 2025 denial, as quoted in a securities class-action complaint. It is a company statement about itself from an earlier period, not an independent finding.

reviews.rationale: No item traces NVIDIA GPU sales through proxies or shell companies to Chinese buyers in the target period. The evidence of diversion covers earlier years, and the only contrary item is NVIDIA's own denial. The packet does not settle the claim.
